record.final_answer:
No, I don't think it would work. Kestrune's own documentation rules out both parts of the plan.

My source is a note saved in memory from an earlier session. It summarises the Kestrune 3.2 limits page (docs.kestrune.example/limits, updated 2026-08-30). I didn't re-read the page today, and the repo doesn't pin a Kestrune version, so check that the version you'd deploy is 3.2 or still has these limits.

According to that page:

1. **Only one writer.** Only one process can open a database for writing; it takes an exclusive file lock, and any other process can only read. With two workers, one on ingest-a and one on ingest-b, both writing (as the `README.md` describes), the second one couldn't get write access.
2. **Local disks only.** The data directory has to be on a local filesystem. NFS and SMB/CIFS aren't supported and "may corrupt the database". `/mnt/shared/ingest` (`config/worker.toml:2`) is an NFS export from fs-01, so the shared mount is unsupported even with just one writer. File locks over NFS are also unreliable, so the single-writer lock might not reliably stop the second host either. That last point is my inference; the docs don't say it.

The other requirements look fine against the documented limits:
- **Value size:** values up to 6 MiB are under the 8 MiB limit. An anonymous forum post claims large values get cut off when compression is on, but nobody has confirmed it.
- **Durability:** surviving a power loss needs the default `sync="full"`. Don't use `sync="off"`.
- **Speed:** we have no measured figure for 300 writes per second with `sync="full"` and 6 MiB values. The vendor's 1.2M writes/s benchmark used `sync="off"`, tiny values and local NVMe, so it doesn't apply here.

Two setups that would fit Kestrune:
- **One store owner.** One host holds the database on its own local disk. The other host sends its writes there, for example through a small service or the queue, instead of opening the files itself.
- **One store per host.** Each worker keeps its own database on its own local disk. This only works if every part of a batch goes to the same host, for example by routing on batch ID. Otherwise neither host can tell when a batch is complete.

If both hosts really have to write to the NFS share directly, Kestrune is the wrong replacement. You'd need a store built for several writers on a network, or a real database server.
